cards.title: Battle of Plassey
cards.body: **Robert Clive** beat **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, the Nawab of Bengal. The Nawab’s own commander, **Mir Jafar**, had been bought before the fight. He stood still during the battle and was made Nawab after it.

cards.q: Which Nawab of Bengal lost the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
cards.n: He was killed a few days later. So he could not have fought at Buxar, seven years on.

cards.q: Which commander betrayed Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey and became Nawab as his prize?
Who led the Company’s army at Plassey?

cards.title: The battle that was won before it began
cards.body: On 23 June 1757 Siraj-ud-Daulah brought about fifty thousand men to the mango groves of **Plassey**. Clive had about three thousand. It should not have been a fight at all. But the largest part of the Nawab’s army stood under **Mir Jafar**, and Mir Jafar had already made a deal. At noon it rained. The Nawab’s gunpowder got wet; the English had covered theirs. By evening the Nawab was running, and a trading company had a kingdom in its hands.

cards.q: Which battle of 1760 ended French hopes in India, and who won it for the British?
cards.n: He beat the French general Count de Lally. It decided the Third Carnatic War.

cards.title: How the French lost India
cards.body: The British and the French fought three **Carnatic Wars** in the south. The last one was settled at **Wandiwash in 1760**, where **Eyre Coote** beat Count de Lally. Pondicherry fell the next year. The French got it back by treaty, but only as a trading town.

cards.title: Battle of Buxar
cards.body: **Hector Munro** beat three rulers at once: **Mir Qasim** of Bengal, **Shuja-ud-Daulah** of Awadh and the Mughal emperor **Shah Alam II**. Plassey was won by a trick. Buxar was won by fighting.

cards.q: Who commanded the Company’s army at Buxar in 1764?
Name the three rulers who fought the Company together at Buxar.
cards.a: Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II
cards.n: Bengal, Awadh and the Mughal emperor. Siraj-ud-Daulah is the wrong name the examiner likes to add.

cards.q: Which Mughal emperor was beaten at Buxar?
Shuja-ud-Daulah, who fought at Buxar, was the Nawab of which state?

cards.title: Why Buxar matters more than Plassey
cards.body: At Plassey the Company beat one Nawab with the help of a traitor. At **Buxar** it beat the Nawab of Bengal, the Nawab of Awadh and the **Mughal emperor** in an open fight. After Buxar nobody in north India could say no to the Company, and the emperor himself signed away the revenue of Bengal.

cards.title: Treaty of Allahabad
cards.body: One year after Buxar, the emperor **Shah Alam II** gave the Company the **Diwani** of **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**. Diwani means the right to collect the land revenue. **Clive** signed for the Company.

cards.q: What does the word “Diwani” mean?
cards.a: The right to collect land revenue

cards.q: Which treaty gave the Company the Diwani, and in which year?
The Diwani of 1765 covered which three areas?
cards.n: “Orissa” here was only a small strip near Midnapore. The British took the rest of Odisha from the Marathas in 1803.

cards.q: Which Mughal emperor gave the Diwani to the Company?
Who signed the Treaty of Allahabad for the Company?
cards.n: He had come back to India in 1765 for a second term as Governor of Bengal.

cards.title: Two masters in Bengal
cards.body: From **1765 to 1772** Bengal had a **dual government**. The Company took the revenue (the Diwani) but did none of the work of ruling. The Nawab had to keep law and order but had no money. It was Clive’s plan. **Warren Hastings** ended it in 1772.

cards.q: What name is given to Clive’s system in which the Company took Bengal’s revenue and the Nawab kept the administration?
cards.n: It ran from 1765 to 1772.

cards.q: Who ended the dual government of Bengal, and in which year?

cards.title: Permanent Settlement
cards.body: **Lord Cornwallis** fixed the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa **for ever**. The **zamindars** became owners of the land. They kept one part in eleven and paid ten parts to the Company.

cards.q: Who brought in the Permanent Settlement, and in which year?
Under the Permanent Settlement, who became the owners of the land?
Why is the Permanent Settlement called “permanent”?
cards.a: The revenue was fixed for ever

cards.q: Which official, later Governor-General himself, planned the Permanent Settlement with Cornwallis?

cards.title: The sunset law
cards.body: The Permanent Settlement was easy on the Company and hard on everyone else. A zamindar had to pay by **sunset on a fixed day**. If he was late, his estate was sold by auction. So the zamindar pressed the farmer, and the farmer had no one to press.

cards.q: Which two officers are linked with the Ryotwari system?
In which parts of India was the Ryotwari system used?
In the Ryotwari system, who paid the land tax to the government?
cards.n: There was no zamindar in between. The tax was not fixed for ever; it was revised from time to time.

cards.q: Who introduced the Mahalwari system, and in which year?
What is a “mahal” in the Mahalwari system?
cards.n: The whole village paid the tax together, through its headman.

cards.q: In which regions was the Mahalwari system used?
cards.a: North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of central India

cards.title: Three ways to tax the land
cards.body: The Company tried three systems. **Permanent Settlement** (Cornwallis, 1793): the zamindar pays, in Bengal. **Ryotwari** (Munro and Read): the farmer pays, in Madras and Bombay. **Mahalwari** (Holt Mackenzie, 1822): the village pays together, in the north. Ask “who pays?” and you can tell them apart.

cards.q: What word do historians use for the ruin of India’s old crafts under British rule?
cards.n: Cheap machine-made cloth from Britain came in almost free of duty, while Indian cloth was taxed heavily in Britain.

cards.q: Who put forward the “drain of wealth” theory?
cards.n: His book was “Poverty and Un-British Rule in India” (1901).

cards.title: The drain
cards.body: **Dadabhai Naoroji** said Britain was draining India. Every year money left India as salaries, pensions and profits, and nothing came back for it. He called this the **drain of wealth** and wrote it down in “Poverty and Un-British Rule in India“. R. C. Dutt made the same case later.

cards.title: The clerk who took a kingdom
cards.body: **Robert Clive** came to Madras in 1744 as a “writer”, the lowest clerk of the Company. He hated the desk. When war with the French began he changed his pen for a sword, and at **Arcot in 1751** he made his name. Six years later he won **Plassey**. He went home rich, and came back in **1765** as Governor of Bengal to take the **Diwani** from the emperor. A clerk had become the tax collector of the richest land in India.

cards.title: Regulating Act
cards.body: The first time the British Parliament stepped in to control the Company. The Governor of Bengal became the **Governor-General of Bengal**, and **Warren Hastings** was the first. A **Supreme Court** was set up at Calcutta.

cards.q: Which was the first Act of the British Parliament to control the Company’s rule in India?
Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal?
Which Act set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta?
cards.n: The court opened in 1774.

cards.q: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta?
Which Act set up the Board of Control to watch the Company from London?

cards.title: Two masters in London
cards.body: After **Pitt’s India Act (1784)** the Company had two bosses at home. The **Court of Directors** looked after trade. The new **Board of Control**, made up of ministers, looked after political matters. This “double government” lasted until 1858.

cards.title: Charter Act
cards.body: The Company lost its **monopoly of trade** with India; it kept only tea and the China trade. **One lakh rupees a year** was set aside for education. Christian missionaries were allowed to come and preach.

cards.q: Which Act ended the Company’s monopoly of trade with India?
cards.n: It kept the monopoly in tea and in trade with China for twenty more years.

cards.q: How much money did the Charter Act of 1813 set aside each year for education?
Which Charter Act first allowed Christian missionaries to work in India?

cards.title: One lakh rupees and twenty-two years
cards.body: In **1813** Parliament told the Company to spend **one lakh rupees a year** on teaching Indians. Then nobody could agree what to teach. One group, the Orientalists, wanted Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian. The other, the Anglicists, wanted English and Western science. The money lay almost unused while they argued. The quarrel ended only in **1835**, when **Macaulay** wrote his famous Minute and **Bentinck** chose English.

cards.q: Which Act turned the Governor-General of Bengal into the Governor-General of India?
Who was the first Governor-General of India?
Who was the first Law Member of the Governor-General’s council?
cards.n: The post was created by the Charter Act of 1833.

cards.q: After which Act did the Company stop trading altogether and remain only a ruler?

cards.title: Three firsts, three Acts
cards.body: **Warren Hastings** was the first Governor-General of Bengal (Act of 1773). **William Bentinck** was the first Governor-General of India (Act of 1833). **Lord Canning** was the first Viceroy (Act of 1858). The examiner swaps the three names, so learn each with its Act.

cards.q: Which Act opened the civil service to competition?
Which committee of 1854 planned the civil service examination?
Who was the first Indian to pass the Indian Civil Service examination, and in which year?
cards.n: He was an elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore.

cards.title: An exam six thousand miles away
cards.body: From **1853** anyone could sit the civil service exam. In practice an Indian had to sail to **London**, write papers in English and compete with boys from English schools. **Satyendranath Tagore** did it in **1863**. Then the rulers made it harder. **Lytton** cut the top age to nineteen. Indians asked for decades that the exam be held in India too. That wish came true only in **1922**, at Allahabad.

cards.title: Government of India Act
cards.body: After the Revolt the **Crown** took India from the Company. A new minister, the **Secretary of State for India**, sat in London with a **council of 15**. The Governor-General was also called the **Viceroy**.

cards.q: Which office was created in London by the Government of India Act, 1858?
How many members sat in the Council of the Secretary of State for India?
Who was the first Viceroy of India?
cards.n: He was also the last Governor-General under the Company.

cards.q: In which city was the Queen’s Proclamation of 1858 read out?
cards.n: Lord Canning read it on 1 November 1858.

cards.q: Which two London bodies were ended by the Act of 1858?
cards.a: The Board of Control and the Court of Directors

cards.q: Which Act first brought Indians into the law-making council?
cards.n: They were chosen by the Viceroy, not elected.

cards.q: Which Act made the first small start with elections to the councils?
cards.n: The word “election” was not used. Local bodies sent up names. Members could also discuss the budget.

cards.q: Which Act gave separate electorates to Muslims?
cards.n: It is also called the Morley–Minto reforms.

cards.q: In the Morley–Minto reforms, which post did Morley hold and which did Minto hold?
cards.a: Morley: Secretary of State. Minto: Viceroy.

cards.q: Who was the first Indian member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council?
cards.n: He joined as Law Member in 1909.

cards.title: Separate electorates
cards.body: In a **separate electorate**, Muslim voters alone chose the Muslim members. The **Act of 1909** began it. The Viceroy, **Lord Minto**, is called the father of communal electorates. The idea grew with every later Act and ended in Partition.

cards.q: Which Act brought dyarchy to the provinces?
cards.n: It is also called the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms.

cards.q: What does “dyarchy” mean?
cards.n: Provincial subjects were cut into two lists: “reserved” for the Governor’s officials and “transferred” for Indian ministers.

cards.q: In the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms, which post did Montagu hold and which did Chelmsford hold?
cards.a: Montagu: Secretary of State. Chelmsford: Viceroy.

cards.q: Which Act first gave the Centre a legislature with two Houses?

cards.title: Dyarchy in one picture
cards.body: Under the **Act of 1919** each province had two kinds of subject. **Reserved** subjects, such as police and land revenue, stayed with the Governor and his officials. **Transferred** subjects, such as education and health, went to Indian ministers. The ministers had the work but not the money.

cards.title: Government of India Act
cards.body: The longest Act the British ever wrote for India. It gave **provincial autonomy**, planned an all-India federation, set up a **Federal Court** and separated **Burma** from India. Much of our Constitution was taken from it.

cards.q: Which Act gave autonomy to the provinces?
In which year did the Federal Court begin work?
cards.n: It was set up under the Act of 1935 and sat in Delhi.

cards.q: Which country was separated from India by the Act of 1935?
Which two new provinces were made in 1936?
On which date did Odisha become a separate province?
cards.n: The day is kept as Utkal Dibasa.

cards.q: The Act of 1935 ended dyarchy in the provinces. Where did it plan to bring dyarchy instead?
cards.n: This part never came into force, because the princes did not join the federation.

cards.title: The ladder in one breath
cards.body: **1773** Governor-General of Bengal. **1784** Board of Control. **1813** trade monopoly ends. **1833** Governor-General of India. **1853** open competition. **1858** Crown rule. **1861** Indians in council. **1892** first elections. **1909** separate electorates. **1919** dyarchy. **1935** provincial autonomy.

cards.title: Delhi Durbar
cards.body: **Lord Lytton** held a grand durbar at Delhi to declare **Queen Victoria the Empress of India**. A terrible famine was killing people in the south at the same time.

cards.q: Which Viceroy held the Delhi Durbar of 1877?
What was announced at the Delhi Durbar of 1877?
cards.a: Queen Victoria was declared Empress of India

cards.q: Which Viceroy passed the Vernacular Press Act, and in which year?
Which other Act of 1878 stopped Indians from keeping weapons without a licence?
The Vernacular Press Act applied to newspapers in which languages?
cards.n: English papers were left alone. That is why it was called the “Gagging Act“.

cards.q: Lytton cut the top age for the civil service exam from 21 to what?

cards.title: Lytton’s black list
cards.body: Learn **Lord Lytton (1876–80)** as the Viceroy who made India angry. He held the **Delhi Durbar (1877)** during a famine. He passed the **Vernacular Press Act** and the **Arms Act** in 1878. He cut the civil service age to 19. Each one gave the early nationalists something to fight.

cards.title: The paper that changed its language overnight
cards.body: The **Vernacular Press Act of 1878** was aimed at Indian-language papers. The sharpest of them was the **Amrita Bazar Patrika** of **Sisir Kumar Ghosh**, printed in Bengali. The Act could not touch an English paper. So the brothers who ran it did a simple thing. The very next issue came out fully in **English**. The law had nothing to hold on to, and the paper went on scolding the government for many more years.

cards.title: Ripon’s Resolution
cards.body: **Lord Ripon** asked for local boards in towns and districts, with most members elected and not chosen by officials. For this he is called the **Father of Local Self-Government** in India.

cards.q: Which Viceroy is called the Father of Local Self-Government in India?
cards.n: The name comes from his Resolution of 1882.

cards.q: Who repealed the Vernacular Press Act, and in which year?
In which year was the first Factory Act passed, and under which Viceroy?
cards.n: It was meant to protect child workers.

cards.q: What did the Ilbert Bill of 1883 try to allow?
Who was Ilbert, after whom the Ilbert Bill is named?
cards.a: The Law Member of Ripon’s council
cards.n: His full name was Courtenay Ilbert.

cards.q: Which education commission did Ripon appoint in 1882?
cards.n: It looked mainly at primary and secondary schools.

cards.q: The first regular census of all India was taken in which year?
cards.n: A first try was made in 1872 under Lord Mayo. From 1881 it has been held every ten years.

cards.title: What the Ilbert Bill taught India
cards.body: The Europeans in India rose in anger against the **Ilbert Bill**, and **Ripon** had to weaken it. Indians watched and learnt a lesson: a noisy, organised protest can bend the government. Two years later, in 1885, the Congress was born.

cards.title: Lytton and Ripon side by side
cards.body: **Lytton** passed the Vernacular Press Act (1878); **Ripon** repealed it (1882). Lytton passed the Arms Act; Ripon passed the first **Factory Act (1881)**. Lytton held a durbar; Ripon gave **local self-government (1882)**, the **Hunter Commission (1882)** and the **Ilbert Bill (1883)**.

cards.title: Wood’s Despatch
cards.body: **Charles Wood** asked for a full ladder of schools, from the village school to the university, and for a department of education in every province. It is called the **Magna Carta of English Education in India**.

cards.q: What is called the Magna Carta of English Education in India?
Which post did Charles Wood hold when he sent his Despatch?
cards.a: President of the Board of Control

cards.q: Which three universities opened in 1857?
Who was the Governor-General when Wood’s Despatch arrived?

cards.title: Macaulay’s Minute
cards.body: **Macaulay** argued that the government’s money should go to teaching Western learning through **English**. The Governor-General, **William Bentinck**, agreed, and English became the language of higher education.

cards.q: What did Macaulay’s Minute of 1835 decide?
cards.a: English would be the language of teaching

cards.q: Which Governor-General accepted Macaulay’s Minute?

cards.title: The downward filter
cards.body: Macaulay did not plan to teach every Indian. He wanted to educate a small class in English and let knowledge “filter down” from them to the people. This is called the **downward filtration theory**. Wood’s Despatch of 1854 gave it up and asked for mass schooling.

cards.q: Put these in order of time: Sadler, Hunter, Hartog, Raleigh.
Put these in order of time: Kothari, Sargent, Radhakrishnan, Wardha scheme.
The Raleigh Commission of 1902 looked at what, and which Viceroy appointed it?
cards.n: It led to the Indian Universities Act of 1904.

cards.q: The Sadler Commission of 1917 studied which university?
By what other name is the Wardha scheme of 1937 known?
cards.n: It was Gandhi’s idea: learning through a craft, in the mother tongue. A committee under Zakir Husain worked it out.

cards.q: Which was the first education commission of free India, and in which year?
cards.n: It looked at university education.

cards.q: Which commission of 1964–66 gave the 10+2+3 pattern?
The Hartog Committee of 1929 was a branch of which larger commission?

cards.title: Eight names in a row
cards.body: The 2025 paper asked the order of the education commissions. Say it as one line: **Hunter 1882, Raleigh 1902, Sadler 1917, Hartog 1929, Wardha 1937, Sargent 1944, Radhakrishnan 1948, Kothari 1964**. The first four are British-era bodies. Wardha is Gandhi’s. The last two belong to free India.

cards.q: Which is counted as the first political association of modern India, and in which year was it founded?
cards.n: Dwarkanath Tagore was among its founders. It spoke for the zamindars of Bengal.

cards.q: Who founded the Mohammedan Literary Society in Calcutta in 1863?
Who founded the East India Association, where and in which year?

cards.title: Mr Narrow Majority
cards.body: **Dadabhai Naoroji** believed the British public would be fair if only it knew the truth about India. So he went to live among them. In **1866** he started the **East India Association** in London. In **1892** he stood for the British Parliament from Finsbury and won by a handful of votes, so few that people joked and called him “Mr Narrow Majority“. He was the **first Indian member of the House of Commons**. India called him the **Grand Old Man**.

cards.q: Who was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons?
cards.n: He won in 1892. He is called the Grand Old Man of India.

cards.q: Which association was founded at Poona in 1870, and who is the name linked with it?
cards.a: Poona Sarvajanik Sabha; M. G. Ranade

cards.title: Indian Association
cards.body: **Surendranath Banerjea** and **Ananda Mohan Bose** started it in Calcutta. It was the strongest political body before the Congress, and it led the protest when the civil service age was cut.

cards.q: Who founded the Indian Association in 1876?
cards.a: Surendranath Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose

cards.q: Who founded the Central National Mohammedan Association?
cards.n: He founded it in Calcutta in 1877.

cards.q: Which two associations were founded just before the Congress, in 1884 and 1885?
cards.a: Madras Mahajan Sabha and Bombay Presidency Association

cards.title: The elder brothers of the Congress
cards.body: Say them by year. **1863** Mohammedan Literary Society (Abdul Latif). **1866** East India Association (Naoroji). **1870** Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (Ranade). **1876** Indian Association (Banerjea). **1884** Madras Mahajan Sabha. **1885** Bombay Presidency Association. Then the Congress.

cards.title: Indian National Congress
cards.body: The first session met at **Bombay** in December 1885 with **72 delegates**. **W. C. Bonnerjee** was the president. A retired British officer, **A. O. Hume**, had brought the leaders together.

cards.q: Where was the first session of the Indian National Congress held, and who presided?
Which retired British civil servant helped to found the Congress?
Who was the Viceroy when the Congress was founded in 1885?
Which newspaper did Raja Rammohan Roy run?
Dadabhai Naoroji ran which newspaper?
Who founded The Hindu?
cards.n: It began in Madras in 1878.

cards.q: Who founded the Amrita Bazar Patrika?
Name Tilak’s two newspapers and the language of each.
Which two papers did Annie Besant run?
Who ran the newspaper Al-Hilal?
Who ran the newspaper Comrade?
cards.n: The examiner swaps Comrade and Al-Hilal. Comrade was English; Al-Hilal was Urdu.

cards.q: Name two newspapers that Gandhi ran in India.
cards.n: He also ran Navajivan in Gujarati, and Indian Opinion in South Africa.

cards.q: Which newspaper did Dr Ambedkar start in 1920?

cards.title: A paper and its owner
cards.body: The examiner gives a newspaper and asks the owner. Pair them: **Sambad Kaumudi** and Rammohan Roy. **Rast Goftar** and Naoroji. **Kesari** and Tilak. **New India** and Besant. **Al-Hilal** and Azad. **Comrade** and Mohammad Ali. **Young India** and Gandhi. **Mook Nayak** and Ambedkar.

cards.q: Which was the first Odia newspaper, and who started it?
cards.n: It began in 1866, the year of the great famine.

cards.q: Who started The Samaja, and in which year?

cards.title: Utkal Dipika
cards.body: **Gourishankar Ray** brought out the first newspaper in Odia from Cuttack. It began in the year of the Na’anka famine and spoke up for the Odia language and for famine relief.

cards.q: Which was the first newspaper printed in India, and in which year?

cards.title: The first editor went to jail
cards.body: India’s first newspaper was a small weekly started at Calcutta in **1780** by an Irishman, **James Augustus Hicky**. He called it the **Bengal Gazette**. Hicky printed gossip about the Company’s officers and then went after the Governor-General himself, **Warren Hastings**. He was fined and jailed, and in 1782 his types were seized. The paper lived only two years. But it set the pattern for a hundred years: Indian papers and the government were never friends.

cards.q: Which Governor-General brought in press censorship in 1799?
Who is called the Liberator of the Indian Press, and why?
cards.a: Charles Metcalfe; he removed the press curbs in 1835

cards.q: Who made a licence compulsory for every press in 1823?

cards.title: Four press laws
cards.body: **1799** Wellesley brings censorship, in fear of the French. **1823** John Adam makes a licence compulsory. **1835** Charles Metcalfe frees the press. **1878** Lytton gags the Indian-language papers. Tight, tighter, free, tight again.

cards.q: Who called Tilak the “Father of Indian Unrest”?
cards.n: He was a British journalist. He said it in his book “Indian Unrest” (1910).

cards.q: Valentine Chirol’s book “Indian Unrest” gave a famous title to which leader?

cards.title: An insult worn as a medal
cards.body: In 1910 a British journalist, **Valentine Chirol**, wrote a book to explain why India was angry. He blamed one man and called him the **Father of Indian Unrest**. **Tilak** went to London and took him to court for it. He lost the case and a great deal of money. But in India the insult was read as praise. If the British thought one man had woken the country, that man must be worth following.

cards.q: Which slogan is Tilak remembered for?
cards.a: “Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it”

cards.q: By which title, meaning “honoured by the people”, is Tilak known?
Which two festivals did Tilak turn into public gatherings?
cards.a: The Ganapati festival and the Shivaji festival
cards.n: Ganapati in 1893 and Shivaji in 1895. A religious crowd could meet where a political one could not.

cards.q: In which jail was Tilak kept from 1908 to 1914, and which book did he write there?
Tilak died on 1 August 1920. Which movement began on that same day?

cards.title: Tilak in five lines
cards.body: Newspapers: **Kesari** (Marathi) and **Mahratta** (English). Festivals: Ganapati and Shivaji. Slogan: “Swaraj is my birthright“. Jail: **Mandalay**, 1908–14, where he wrote **Gita Rahasya**. Last work: the **Home Rule League** and the **Lucknow Pact**, both 1916.

cards.q: Who were Lal, Bal and Pal?
cards.a: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal
cards.n: Punjab, Maharashtra and Bengal. They led the Extremists in the Congress.

cards.q: Bipin Chandra Pal belonged to which province?
cards.n: He edited New India and worked on Bande Mataram.

cards.title: Moderates and Extremists
cards.body: The **Moderates**, such as Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta, sent petitions and trusted British fairness. The **Extremists**, **Lal, Bal and Pal**, wanted boycott, swadeshi and mass action. The two groups broke apart at **Surat in 1907** and came together again at **Lucknow in 1916**.

cards.title: Surat split
cards.body: The Congress broke in two at its Surat session. The Moderates kept the party; the Extremists under Tilak were shut out for nine years. **Rash Behari Ghosh** was the president of the session.

cards.q: At which session did the Congress split into Moderates and Extremists, and in which year?
Who presided over the Surat session of 1907?

cards.title: Partition of Bengal
cards.body: **Lord Curzon** cut Bengal in two. He said the province was too big to govern. Indians saw a plan to divide Hindus and Muslims. The answer was the **Swadeshi movement**: boycott foreign cloth, buy Indian.

cards.q: Which Viceroy partitioned Bengal in 1905?
Which movement began as the answer to the Partition of Bengal?
In which year was the Partition of Bengal cancelled, and what else was announced with it?
cards.a: 1911; the capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi
cards.n: Lord Hardinge was the Viceroy. King George V announced it at the Delhi Durbar.

cards.q: Where and in which year was the Muslim League founded?

cards.title: Two Home Rule Leagues
cards.body: **Tilak** started his league in April, for Maharashtra and Karnataka. **Annie Besant** started hers in September from Madras, for the rest of India. Both asked for self-government inside the British Empire.

cards.q: Who started the two Home Rule Leagues of 1916?
cards.n: Tilak’s came first, in April. Besant’s followed in September.

cards.q: What did the Lucknow Pact of 1916 bring together?
cards.a: The Congress and the Muslim League
cards.n: At the same session the Moderates and Extremists also came back together.

cards.q: Who presided over the Lucknow session of 1916?
Which leader is called “Punjab Kesari”?
Which newspaper did Lala Lajpat Rai found?
Who was the first president of the All India Trade Union Congress?
cards.n: The year was 1920.

cards.q: Lala Lajpat Rai died of injuries received in a protest against what?
cards.n: The police lathi-charged the march at Lahore in October 1928. He died on 17 November.

cards.q: Which society did Lala Lajpat Rai found?
cards.n: Do not mix it up with Gokhale’s Servants of India Society (1905).

cards.title: The blows at Lahore
cards.body: On 30 October 1928 the Simon Commission reached Lahore station. A silent crowd stood there with black flags, led by an old man, **Lala Lajpat Rai**. The police charged with lathis and the blows fell on his chest. That evening he said that every blow on his body would prove a nail in the coffin of British rule. He died on **17 November**. A month later a young man named **Bhagat Singh** shot a police officer, Saunders, in revenge.

cards.q: Who founded the Servants of India Society, and in which year?
Whom did Gandhi call his political guru?

cards.title: Gandhi comes home
cards.body: Gandhi landed at Bombay from South Africa on **9 January 1915**. The day is now kept as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas. On Gokhale’s advice he spent a year travelling and listening before he spoke on Indian politics.

cards.q: On which date did Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
cards.n: The day is now Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.

cards.q: Put in order: Kheda, Champaran, Rowlatt Satyagraha, Ahmedabad Mill Strike.

cards.title: Four small fights
cards.body: Gandhi tested satyagraha four times before he used it on the whole country. **Champaran 1917**: indigo farmers. **Ahmedabad 1918**: mill workers, and his first hunger strike. **Kheda 1918**: farmers who could not pay tax. **Rowlatt 1919**: his first all-India call.

cards.q: Which was Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India, and in which year?
The Champaran satyagraha was fought for farmers forced to grow which crop?
cards.n: Under the “tinkathia” system a farmer had to grow indigo on three parts in twenty of his land.

cards.q: Champaran is in which State?

cards.title: The farmer who would not go away
cards.body: In 1916 a farmer from Champaran named **Rajkumar Shukla** came to the Lucknow Congress. He wanted someone to see how the indigo planters treated his people. He picked Gandhi, who had never heard of Champaran. Shukla followed him to Kanpur, then to Ahmedabad, then to Calcutta, asking each time. At last Gandhi gave in. In **1917** he reached Champaran, refused an order to leave, and won. It was his **first satyagraha in India**.

cards.q: In which struggle did Gandhi go on his first hunger strike?
cards.n: The mill workers were asking for higher wages. They got a 35 per cent rise.

cards.q: What was the Kheda satyagraha of 1918 about?
cards.a: Farmers refused to pay land tax after their crops failed

cards.q: Kheda is in which State, and which future leader joined Gandhi there?
What did the Rowlatt Act of 1919 allow the government to do?
cards.n: People called it the Black Act: “no appeal, no lawyer, no argument“.

cards.title: Jallianwala Bagh
cards.body: On **13 April**, the day of Baisakhi, **General Dyer** closed the only way out of a walled garden at Amritsar and ordered his men to fire on the crowd. **Tagore** gave up his knighthood in protest.

cards.q: On which date did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place?
Who ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh?
Who gave up his knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh?
cards.n: Gandhi gave back his Kaiser-i-Hind medal.

cards.q: Which committee inquired into the Jallianwala Bagh firing?
cards.n: This is a different Hunter from the education commission of 1882.

cards.q: Put in order: Quit India, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Simon Commission boycott.
cards.a: Non-Cooperation, Simon boycott, Civil Disobedience, Quit India

cards.title: Three movements, three endings
cards.body: **Non-Cooperation (1920–22)** ended when Gandhi called it off after Chauri Chaura. **Civil Disobedience (1930–34)** began with salt and paused with the Gandhi–Irwin Pact. **Quit India (1942)** had no pause: the leaders were jailed on the first morning and the people carried on alone.

cards.q: After which event did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement?
cards.n: A crowd set fire to a police station in Gorakhpur district and 22 policemen died.

cards.q: Which party did C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru form in 1923, after Non-Cooperation was called off?
Why did Indians boycott the Simon Commission?
cards.n: All seven members were British. It came in 1928 and was met with “Simon Go Back“.

cards.title: Dandi March
cards.body: Gandhi left **Sabarmati Ashram** on **12 March** with **78 followers**. He walked for 24 days to the sea at Dandi and picked up salt on **6 April**. That one act began the Civil Disobedience Movement.

cards.q: On which date did Gandhi break the salt law at Dandi?
From which place did the Dandi March begin?
cards.n: It began on 12 March 1930 with 78 followers.

cards.q: Which movement began with the Dandi March?

cards.title: Odisha’s Dandi
cards.body: When Gandhi marched to Dandi, Odisha marched too. A party set out from Cuttack under **Gopabandhu Choudhury** and **Acharya Harihar** for **Inchudi** on the Balasore coast, and salt was made there in April 1930. Inchudi is remembered as the second great centre of the salt satyagraha after Dandi.

cards.q: Which place in Balasore district was the centre of the salt satyagraha in Odisha?
Which pact of March 1931 paused the Civil Disobedience Movement?
Which Round Table Conference did Gandhi attend?
cards.n: He went as the only speaker for the Congress. The Congress stayed away from the first and the third.

cards.q: What did the Poona Pact of 1932 settle, and between whom?
cards.a: Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes; Gandhi and Ambedkar
cards.n: Ambedkar gave up separate electorates in return for more reserved seats.

cards.q: Which was the only Congress session over which Gandhi presided?
Who presided over the Lahore session of 1929, and what goal was adopted there?
On which date was the first Independence Day kept?
cards.n: That is why the Constitution came into force on 26 January, twenty years later.

cards.q: Which Congress session was the first to be held in a village?
At which session did Subhas Bose defeat Pattabhi Sitaramayya?
cards.n: Sitaramayya was Gandhi’s choice. Bose won, then resigned, and formed the Forward Bloc.

cards.q: Who was the first woman president of the Congress, and who was the first Indian woman?

cards.title: Sessions worth one mark each
cards.body: **Belgaum 1924**: Gandhi’s only time as president. **Lahore 1929**: Nehru, Purna Swaraj. **Karachi 1931**: Patel, Fundamental Rights. **Faizpur 1936**: first village session. **Haripura 1938** and **Tripuri 1939**: Subhas Bose.

cards.title: Karachi session
cards.body: It met days after **Bhagat Singh** was hanged. **Sardar Patel** presided. The session approved the Gandhi–Irwin Pact and passed the resolution on **Fundamental Rights** and the National Economic Programme.

cards.q: Who presided over the Karachi session of 1931?
cards.n: The 2025 paper offered Motilal Nehru. He had died in February 1931, before the session met.

cards.q: Which famous resolution was passed at the Karachi session of 1931?
cards.a: Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme

cards.q: On which date were Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru hanged?

cards.title: Quit India
cards.body: On **8 August** the Congress met at Bombay and asked the British to leave at once. Gandhi gave the call **“Do or Die”**. By the next morning every leader was in jail.

cards.q: Which slogan did Gandhi give with the Quit India resolution?
In which city, and on which date, was the Quit India resolution passed?
The failure of which mission in 1942 led to the Quit India Movement?

cards.title: AITUC
cards.body: The **All India Trade Union Congress** was founded at **Bombay**. It was the first all-India body of workers. **Lala Lajpat Rai** was its first president.

cards.q: In which year and in which city was the All India Trade Union Congress founded?
Which labour leader, named in the 2025 paper, was one of the builders of the AITUC?
Who founded the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association?
Which Act of 1926 gave trade unions a legal standing?
Who founded the Communist Party of India, and where?
cards.n: The year was 1920. A party inside India was formed later, at Kanpur in 1925.

cards.title: The man with many names
cards.body: He was born Narendranath Bhattacharya in Bengal. In 1915 he left India to find guns for a revolt, and the search took him across the world. In America he took a new name, **M. N. Roy**. In Mexico he helped to start a communist party. In Moscow he argued with Lenin. And in **1920**, at **Tashkent** in Central Asia, he founded the **Communist Party of India** with a few other exiles. The party was born thousands of miles from the country it was named after.

cards.q: In which year and in which province was the Labour Swaraj Party formed?
Name the three leaders of the Labour Swaraj Party.
cards.a: Muzaffar Ahmed, Qazi Nazrul Islam and Hemanta Kumar Sarkar
cards.n: S. A. Dange is the trap. He worked in Bombay and was not in this party.

cards.q: Which famous poet was among the founders of the Labour Swaraj Party?
In which conspiracy case of 1924 were Dange and Muzaffar Ahmed tried?

cards.title: Meerut Conspiracy Case
cards.body: In March the government arrested about thirty labour leaders in one sweep, among them **Muzaffar Ahmed, S. A. Dange and P. C. Joshi**, and three Englishmen. The trial dragged on until 1933.

cards.q: In which year did the Meerut Conspiracy Case begin?
Name three well-known accused in the Meerut Conspiracy Case.
cards.a: Muzaffar Ahmed, S. A. Dange and P. C. Joshi

cards.q: The Meerut Conspiracy Case was aimed at which group of people?

cards.title: Why Meerut?
cards.body: The arrested leaders worked in Bombay and Calcutta. In those cities they would have been tried before a **jury**, and a jury might have let them go. So the government held the trial in the small town of **Meerut**, where no jury was needed. The plan failed. The long trial made the accused famous across India.

cards.title: Two cases, five years apart
cards.body: **Kanpur 1924**: a few communists, among them Dange and Muzaffar Ahmed, were tried for plotting against the King. **Meerut 1929**: about thirty labour leaders, with the same two names again, plus P. C. Joshi and three Englishmen. Both cases tried to crush the Left and both made it better known.

cards.q: Who formed the Congress Socialist Party, and in which year?
cards.a: Jayaprakash Narayan and Acharya Narendra Dev, 1934
cards.n: It worked inside the Congress, not against it.

cards.q: Where and in which year was the All India Kisan Sabha formed, and who was its first president?

cards.title: The Left in five dates
cards.body: **1920** AITUC, and the CPI at Tashkent. **1925** Labour Swaraj Party in Bengal. **1929** Meerut Conspiracy Case. **1934** Congress Socialist Party. **1936** All India Kisan Sabha.

cards.q: What was the Kakori case of 1925 about?
cards.a: Revolutionaries robbed a train carrying government money
cards.n: Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqulla Khan were hanged for it.

cards.q: The Alipore Conspiracy Case of 1908 was against which leader, and who defended him?
The Lahore Conspiracy Case was the trial of whom?
cards.n: It followed the killing of the police officer Saunders in 1928.

cards.title: Do not mix up the cases
cards.body: **Alipore 1908**: Aurobindo Ghosh, bombs in Bengal. **Kanpur 1924**: communists. **Kakori 1925**: a train robbery by revolutionaries. **Lahore**: Bhagat Singh. **Meerut 1929**: labour leaders. Ask “who was in the dock?” and each case stands apart.

cards.q: Bhagat Singh and B. K. Dutt threw bombs in the Central Assembly in 1929. Which two Bills were they protesting against?
cards.a: The Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill
cards.n: Both Bills were aimed at the labour movement. The bombs were made to make noise, not to kill.

cards.title: The first INA
cards.body: Singapore fell to Japan in February and thousands of Indian soldiers became prisoners. **Captain Mohan Singh** raised the first **Indian National Army** from them, with Japanese help.

cards.q: Who raised the first Indian National Army, and in which year?
cards.n: Netaji came later. He rebuilt the army in 1943.

cards.q: The first INA was raised from which group of men?
cards.a: Indian prisoners of war held by Japan

cards.q: Who led the Indian Independence League?
cards.n: He had planned the bomb attack on the Viceroy, Lord Hardinge, in 1912, and fled to Japan in 1915.

cards.title: Two Boses
cards.body: **Rash Behari Bose** was the old revolutionary in Japan who led the **Indian Independence League**. **Subhas Chandra Bose** was the Congress leader who escaped from India in 1941. In 1943 the elder Bose handed the League and the army to the younger one. They were not related.

cards.q: In which year did Subhas Chandra Bose escape from his house in Calcutta?

cards.title: Twice elected, once escaped
cards.body: **Subhas Chandra Bose** was elected Congress president at **Haripura in 1938**, and again at **Tripuri in 1939** against Gandhi’s own candidate. The party’s leaders would not work with him, so he resigned and formed the **Forward Bloc**. The British shut him in his own house in Calcutta. One night in January **1941** he slipped out in disguise. He crossed Afghanistan and reached Berlin. Two years later a submarine carried him half-way round the world to lead an army.

cards.q: Which party did Subhas Bose form in 1939 after leaving the Congress presidency?
How did Subhas Bose travel from Germany to East Asia in 1943?

cards.title: Provisional Government of Free India
cards.body: **Subhas Chandra Bose** announced it at **Singapore** on **21 October**. It is also called the Azad Hind government. Japan handed it the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

cards.q: On which date and in which city did Netaji announce the Provisional Government of Free India?
Which two war cries did Netaji give the INA?
What was the women’s unit of the INA called, and who led it?
cards.a: Rani of Jhansi Regiment; Lakshmi Sahgal

cards.q: What names did Netaji give to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands?
Complete Netaji’s line: “Give me blood, and I will give you ...”
Up to which two towns in north-east India did the INA advance in 1944?

cards.title: Red Fort trials
cards.body: The British tried three INA officers at the Red Fort in Delhi: **Shah Nawaz Khan, P. K. Sehgal and G. S. Dhillon**. **Bhulabhai Desai** led the defence. The whole country took their side.

cards.q: Name the three INA officers tried at the Red Fort in 1945.
cards.a: Shah Nawaz Khan, P. K. Sehgal and G. S. Dhillon

cards.q: Who led the defence in the INA trials at the Red Fort?
cards.n: Nehru, Tej Bahadur Sapru and Asaf Ali were also on the defence team.

cards.title: Three men in the dock
cards.body: When the war ended the British wanted to make an example of the INA. They chose three officers and tried them in public at the **Red Fort**. By chance, or by carelessness, the three were a Muslim, a Hindu and a Sikh: **Shah Nawaz Khan, Sehgal and Dhillon**. Nothing could have joined India faster. Crowds shouted their names in every town, and **Nehru** put on his lawyer’s gown after many years. The men were found guilty and then quietly set free.

cards.q: In which year did the sailors of the Royal Indian Navy revolt at Bombay?
Where was the Ghadar Party founded, and in which year?
cards.n: Lala Har Dayal was its moving spirit. Sohan Singh Bhakna was its first president.

cards.q: Who founded the Free India Society in London?
Who founded India House in London in 1905?
Who raised an Indian flag at Stuttgart in Germany in 1907?

cards.title: Two governments in exile
cards.body: Netaji’s government of **1943** at Singapore was not the first. In **1915** a Provisional Government of India was set up at **Kabul**, with **Raja Mahendra Pratap** as President and **Barkatullah** as Prime Minister. If the question says “first”, the answer is Kabul.

cards.q: Who was the President of the Provisional Government of India set up at Kabul in 1915?

cards.title: The Constituent Assembly meets
cards.body: The Assembly sat for the first time on **9 December 1946**. The oldest member, **Sachchidananda Sinha**, took the chair for two days. Then **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was elected its President.

cards.q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly first meet?
Who was the temporary President of the Constituent Assembly at its first meeting?
cards.n: He was the oldest member. Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected President two days later.

cards.q: Who was the elected President of the Constituent Assembly?
Under which plan of 1946 was the Constituent Assembly set up?
Who first put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India, in 1934?
Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee?
cards.n: The committee was set up on 29 August 1947 and had seven members.

cards.q: Who was the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly?
cards.n: He studied about sixty constitutions and prepared the first draft for the Drafting Committee to work on.

cards.q: How long did the Constituent Assembly take to make the Constitution?
On which date was the Constitution adopted, and on which date did it come into force?
cards.n: 26 November is kept as Constitution Day.

cards.title: The book when it was new
cards.body: The Constitution of 1950 had **395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules**. Today it has **12 Schedules**. It is the longest written constitution in the world, because one book holds the rules for both the Centre and the States.

cards.q: How many Articles, Parts and Schedules did the original Constitution have?

cards.title: The adviser nobody remembers
cards.body: Everyone knows Dr Ambedkar wrote the Constitution. Fewer know the man who gave him the first draft. **B. N. Rau** was a civil servant and a judge, and the Assembly made him its **Constitutional Adviser**. He read the constitutions of about sixty countries. He travelled to America, Canada, Ireland and Britain to ask judges what had gone wrong in theirs. Then he wrote a draft and handed it to the **Drafting Committee**. He took no salary for the work.

cards.q: Which single source gave the Indian Constitution the most?
cards.n: The federal plan, the office of Governor, the Public Service Commissions and the emergency rules came from it.

cards.q: The office of Governor and the Public Service Commissions were taken from which source?
From which country did India take single citizenship?
cards.n: Asked in 2021. The USA has double citizenship: of the country and of a State.

cards.q: The parliamentary system and the rule of law came from which country?
The five writs came to our Constitution from which country?

cards.title: What Britain gave
cards.body: From **Britain** came the way our government works day to day: the **parliamentary system**, the cabinet, the **rule of law**, **single citizenship**, the **writs** and two Houses of Parliament. Britain itself has no single written constitution.

cards.q: From which country did India take the Fundamental Rights?
Judicial review and the independence of the judiciary came from which country?
The impeachment of the President was taken from which country?
cards.n: The post of Vice-President and the removal of judges also came from the USA.

cards.q: Which three things did India take from the Constitution of Ireland?
cards.a: Directive Principles, the method of electing the President, nomination to the Rajya Sabha
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: The idea of nominating members to the Rajya Sabha came from which country?
How many members does the President nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
cards.n: They are people known for literature, science, art and social service.

cards.q: A federation with a strong Centre was taken from which country?
In India, who holds the residuary (left-over) powers, and which country gave this rule?
cards.n: In the USA the left-over powers stay with the States. India chose the opposite.

cards.q: The appointment of State Governors by the Centre follows the model of which country?
From which country did India take the Concurrent List?
The joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament came from which country?
The suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency was taken from which constitution?
The Fundamental Duties were taken from which country?
The procedure for amending the Constitution was taken from which country?
“Procedure established by law” was taken from which country?
“Liberty, equality and fraternity” in the Preamble came from which country?
cards.n: The idea of a republic came from France too.

cards.title: The small loans
cards.body: Five small loans are asked most. **Germany** (Weimar): suspending rights in an Emergency. **USSR**: Fundamental Duties. **South Africa**: how to amend. **Japan**: “procedure established by law“. **France**: liberty, equality, fraternity.

cards.title: Canada or Australia?
cards.body: These two are mixed up most. **Canada** is about power: a strong Centre, left-over powers with the Centre, Governors sent by the Centre. **Australia** is about working together: the **Concurrent List** and the **joint sitting**.

cards.title: Objectives Resolution
cards.body: On **13 December 1946** **Jawaharlal Nehru** moved a resolution saying what kind of country India would be. The Assembly passed it on 22 January 1947. It grew into the Preamble.

cards.q: Who moved the Objectives Resolution, and on which date?
The Preamble grew out of which resolution?
With which words does the Preamble begin?
cards.n: So the power of the Constitution comes from the people, not from Parliament or the States.

cards.q: In the Preamble, what five words describe India, in order?
Which four ideals does the Preamble promise, in order?
Which three kinds of justice does the Preamble name?
cards.n: The order matters. The examiner changes it to “political, social and economic“.

cards.q: The Preamble promises liberty of which five things?
cards.a: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship

cards.q: The Preamble promises equality of which two things?
Which date is written inside the Preamble?

cards.title: The Preamble in one breath
cards.body: India is a **Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic**. It promises **Justice** (social, economic, political), **Liberty** (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), **Equality** (status and opportunity) and **Fraternity** (the dignity of the person and the unity and integrity of the Nation).

cards.q: What does the word “Republic” mean in the Preamble?
cards.a: The head of the State is elected, not a king
cards.n: Britain is a democracy but not a republic.

cards.q: In which case did the Supreme Court say the Preamble is NOT a part of the Constitution?
In which case did the Supreme Court say the Preamble IS a part of the Constitution?
Which doctrine did the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973 lay down?
cards.n: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but it cannot destroy its basic features.

cards.title: Thirteen judges and one head of a monastery
cards.body: **Kesavananda Bharati** was the head of a religious house in Kerala. The State took some of its land, and in 1970 he went to court. He lost his land. But his case grew into the biggest hearing the Supreme Court has ever held: **thirteen judges**, sitting for 68 days. In **1973** they ruled, by seven to six, that Parliament may change the Constitution but may not destroy its **basic structure**. The case carries his name, yet he gained nothing from it.

cards.q: How many judges heard the Kesavananda Bharati case?
cards.n: It is the largest bench the Supreme Court has ever had. The verdict was seven to six.

cards.title: The 42nd Amendment and the Preamble
cards.body: The Preamble has been amended **only once**. During the Emergency the 42nd Amendment added three words: **Socialist, Secular** and **Integrity**.

cards.q: How many times has the Preamble been amended?
Which amendment changed the Preamble, and in which year?
Which three words did the 42nd Amendment add to the Preamble?
cards.n: “Unity of the Nation” became “unity and integrity of the Nation“.

cards.q: Can a citizen go to court to enforce the Preamble?
cards.n: It is a part of the Constitution but it is not enforceable. It gives no power and sets no limit by itself.

cards.q: Who called the Preamble the “key-note” of the Constitution?
Who called the Preamble the “horoscope” of our republic?
Who called the Preamble the “soul” of the Constitution?
Who called the Preamble the “identity card” of the Constitution?

cards.title: Four names for one page
cards.body: **Key-note**: Ernest Barker. **Horoscope**: K. M. Munshi. **Soul**: Thakurdas Bhargava. **Identity card**: N. A. Palkhivala. Do not mix this with Article 32, which **Ambedkar** called the “heart and soul” of the Constitution.

cards.q: Which Part and which Articles of the Constitution hold the Fundamental Rights?
How many Fundamental Rights are there today, and how many were there in 1950?
cards.n: The right to property was taken out in 1978.

cards.title: Six rooms
cards.body: Part III has six groups of rights. **Equality**: Articles 14–18. **Freedom**: 19–22. **Against exploitation**: 23–24. **Religion**: 25–28. **Culture and education**: 29–30. **Constitutional remedies**: 32.

cards.q: Which Articles cover the right to freedom of religion?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: Which Articles cover the right to equality?
Which Articles cover the right against exploitation?
Which Article promises equality before the law?
Which Article abolishes untouchability?
Which Article abolishes titles?
On which five grounds does Article 15 forbid discrimination?
cards.a: Religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth

cards.q: Which Article gives the six freedoms, such as speech and movement?
Name the six freedoms of Article 19.
cards.a: Speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession

cards.q: Which Article protects life and personal liberty?
Which Article makes education a Fundamental Right, and for which ages?
cards.n: It was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

cards.q: Which two Articles cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency?
cards.n: The 44th Amendment made sure of this, after the Emergency of 1975.

cards.q: Which Article bans traffic in human beings and forced labour?
Article 24 bans the work of children below what age in factories and mines?
Which five Articles give rights to citizens only, and not to foreigners?
Can a foreigner in India claim the freedom of speech under Article 19?
cards.n: Article 19 is for citizens only. But a foreigner does have Articles 14 and 21.

cards.title: A tourist’s rights
cards.body: A foreign tourist in Puri has most Fundamental Rights. She is equal before the law (**Article 14**) and her life and liberty are protected (**Article 21**). What she does not have are the five citizen-only Articles: **15, 16, 19, 29 and 30**.

cards.q: In which year did the Supreme Court declare privacy a Fundamental Right, and under which Article?
cards.n: A bench of nine judges decided it in the Puttaswamy case.

cards.title: The growing family of Article 21
cards.body: The courts keep finding new rights inside the words “life and personal liberty“. **Privacy** (2017). **Maternity leave** as part of a woman’s dignity (2025). **Menstrual health** (January 2026) ⟨CHECK⟩. Education got its own number, **21A**.

cards.q: Which amendment removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights?
Under which Article is the right to property now a legal right?
Which Article did Dr Ambedkar call the “heart and soul” of the Constitution?
cards.n: It is the right to go to the Supreme Court to enforce the Fundamental Rights.

cards.q: Under which Articles do the Supreme Court and the High Courts issue writs?
cards.n: A High Court’s power is wider. It can issue writs for other legal rights too.

cards.q: Which Article defines “the State” for the purpose of Fundamental Rights?
Which writ frees a person who is held illegally?
cards.n: The words mean “you shall have the body“.

cards.q: Which writ orders a public official to do his duty?
cards.n: The word means “we command“. Asked in 2018.

cards.q: Which writ stops a lower court in the middle of a case?
Which writ cancels an order that a lower court has already passed?
Which writ asks a person by what authority he holds a public office?

cards.title: Five keys
cards.body: **Habeas Corpus**: produce the person. **Mandamus**: do your duty. **Prohibition**: stop the case now. **Certiorari**: the order is cancelled. **Quo Warranto**: by what right do you hold this post? Prohibition comes before the order; Certiorari comes after it.

cards.q: Which Part and which Articles hold the Directive Principles?
Can a court enforce the Directive Principles?
cards.n: Article 37 says they are not enforceable, but they are “fundamental in the governance of the country“.

cards.title: Rights and Directives
cards.body: A **Fundamental Right** is a limit on the State: the State must not do this. A **Directive Principle** is a goal for the State: the State should try to do this. You can go to court for the first. You can only vote on the second.

cards.q: Which Article asks the State to give free legal aid?
cards.n: It was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

cards.q: Which Article asks the State to organise village panchayats?
Which Article speaks of a uniform civil code?
Which Directive Principle asks for equal pay for equal work for men and women?
Which Article is about early childhood care and education for children below six?
Which Article asks the State to raise the level of nutrition and to ban harmful drinks?
Which Article is about farming, animal husbandry and the protection of cows?
Which Article asks the State to protect the environment, forests and wildlife?
cards.n: It was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

cards.q: Which Article asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive?
Which Article is about international peace and security?
cards.n: It is called the Article on foreign policy. Asked in 2025, with Article 50 as a wrong option.

cards.title: Walking down the corridor
cards.body: Say the numbers once a day. **39A** legal aid. **40** panchayats. **44** uniform civil code. **45** young children. **47** nutrition and prohibition. **48** farming and cows. **48A** environment. **50** separate the judiciary. **51** world peace.

cards.title: The Gandhian ones
cards.body: Some Directive Principles come straight from Gandhi’s ideas: village **panchayats** (40), **cottage industries** (43), the ban on **intoxicating drinks** (47) and the protection of **cows** (48). The examiner asks you to pick the Gandhian principle from a list.

cards.title: Fundamental Duties
cards.body: The **42nd Amendment** added a new Part IVA with one Article, **51A**, listing ten duties of citizens. The **Swaran Singh Committee** had asked for them. The idea came from the USSR.

cards.q: In which Part and which Article are the Fundamental Duties?
Which committee recommended the Fundamental Duties?
How many Fundamental Duties are there now, and which amendment added the last one?
cards.n: The eleventh asks parents to send children aged 6 to 14 to school.

cards.q: How many Schedules does the Constitution have now?
cards.n: It began with eight.

cards.q: What does the First Schedule contain?
cards.a: The names of the States and Union Territories

cards.q: What does the Second Schedule contain?
cards.n: Those of the President, Governors, judges, the Speaker and the CAG.

cards.q: Which Schedule contains the forms of oaths?
cards.n: The 2025 paper put oaths in the Second Schedule to trick you.

cards.q: What does the Fourth Schedule contain?
cards.a: The seats of each State in the Rajya Sabha

cards.q: Which Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in most States?
cards.n: Large parts of Odisha, such as Koraput, Mayurbhanj and Sundargarh, are Fifth Schedule areas.

cards.q: The Sixth Schedule covers the tribal areas of which four States?
What does the Seventh Schedule contain?
cards.a: The Union, State and Concurrent Lists

cards.q: How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule?
cards.n: It began with 14. Odia was one of them from the start.

cards.title: Three lists
cards.body: The **Seventh Schedule** divides the work. **Union List**: defence, railways, banking, foreign affairs. **State List**: police, public health, agriculture. **Concurrent List**: education, forests, marriage. If a Central law and a State law on a Concurrent subject clash, the Central law wins.

cards.q: Police and public health are in which List?
Education is in which List today?
cards.n: The 42nd Amendment moved it there from the State List in 1976.

cards.q: Which Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment in 1951?
cards.n: It was made to protect land reform laws from being struck down by the courts.

cards.q: Which Schedule holds the anti-defection law?
cards.n: It was added by the 52nd Amendment in 1985.

cards.q: The Eleventh Schedule lists how many subjects, and for which bodies?
The Twelfth Schedule lists how many subjects, and for which bodies?

cards.title: Twelve drawers
cards.body: **1** States. **2** Salaries. **3** Oaths. **4** Rajya Sabha seats. **5** Scheduled Areas. **6** Tribal areas of the north-east. **7** Three lists. **8** Languages. **9** Protected laws. **10** Anti-defection. **11** Panchayats. **12** Municipalities.

cards.title: A drawer the courts could not open
cards.body: In 1950 the new States began to take land from the zamindars and give it to farmers. The zamindars went to court, and the courts began to strike the laws down as a breach of the right to property. So in **1951**, with the very **first amendment**, Parliament built a locked drawer: the **Ninth Schedule**. Any law placed in it could not be challenged for breaking Fundamental Rights. It began with 13 laws. In 2007 the Supreme Court said that even this drawer can be opened.

cards.q: Which Article gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution?
Can the two Houses hold a joint sitting to pass a Constitution Amendment Bill?
cards.n: Each House must pass it separately, by a special majority.

cards.title: Three ways to change the book
cards.body: Some parts change by a **simple majority**, like an ordinary law (making a new State, for example). Most parts need a **special majority** in each House. Parts that touch the States, such as the election of the President, also need the agreement of **half the State Legislatures**.

cards.q: What did the 1st Amendment of 1951 add to the Constitution?
Which amendment of 1956 reorganised the States on the basis of language?

cards.title: The 42nd Amendment
cards.body: Passed during the Emergency. It changed so much that it is called a **mini-constitution**. It added three words to the Preamble, the **Fundamental Duties** and free legal aid, and moved education to the Concurrent List.

cards.q: Which amendment is called a “mini-constitution”?
Name three things the 42nd Amendment added to the Constitution.
cards.a: Three words in the Preamble, the Fundamental Duties, free legal aid
cards.n: It also added Article 48A on the environment and moved five subjects, education among them, to the Concurrent List.

cards.title: The 44th Amendment
cards.body: The Janata government undid the worst of the Emergency changes. The **right to property** stopped being a Fundamental Right, and a National Emergency could no longer be declared for “internal disturbance”, only for **armed rebellion**.

cards.q: Which words replaced “internal disturbance” as a ground for National Emergency?
cards.n: The 44th Amendment made the change in 1978.

cards.q: Under which three Articles can an Emergency be declared?
cards.n: A Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.

cards.q: Which amendment brought in the anti-defection law, and in which year?
Which amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18?
Which amendment made Delhi the National Capital Territory?

cards.title: The 73rd and 74th Amendments
cards.body: The 73rd gave **Panchayats** a place in the Constitution and the 74th did the same for **Municipalities**. Both took effect in 1993. **24 April** is kept as National Panchayati Raj Day.

cards.q: Which amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayats, and which to Municipalities?
On which date is National Panchayati Raj Day kept?
cards.n: The 73rd Amendment came into force on 24 April 1993.

cards.q: Which amendment made education a Fundamental Right?
The 91st Amendment limits the Council of Ministers to what share of the Lok Sabha?
cards.n: The same limit applies in a State, with a floor of 12 ministers. Asked in 2025.

cards.q: What did the 99th Amendment set up, and what happened to it?
cards.a: A commission to appoint judges; the Supreme Court struck it down
cards.n: It came into force in 2015 and was struck down the same year. The collegium system came back.

cards.q: Which amendment brought in the Goods and Services Tax?
cards.n: GST began on 1 July 2017.

cards.q: Which amendment gave a 10 per cent quota to the poor among the general category?
Which amendment reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and the Assemblies?

cards.title: Amendments by number
cards.body: **1** Ninth Schedule. **7** States reorganised. **42** mini-constitution. **44** property right removed. **52** anti-defection. **61** voting age 18. **73, 74** local bodies. **86** education. **91** ministers 15%. **101** GST. **103** EWS quota. **106** women’s seats.

cards.q: Under which Article can Parliament change the name of a State?
Is a law that renames a State counted as a Constitution amendment?
cards.n: Article 4 says so. It is an ordinary law passed by a simple majority.

cards.q: Before a Bill to rename a State is introduced, who must recommend it and whose views must be asked?
cards.n: The views of the State Legislature are not binding on Parliament.

cards.q: In which year did Orissa become Odisha?
cards.n: In the same year “Oriya” became “Odia” in the Eighth Schedule, by the 96th Amendment.

cards.title: Two letters, two laws
cards.body: In 2011 the State changed its English name from Orissa to **Odisha**. That needed only an ordinary law of Parliament under **Article 3**. But the language was also to change, from Oriya to **Odia**, and the language sits in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. A Schedule can be changed only by an amendment. So two laws went through Parliament together: a small Act for the State and the **96th Amendment** for the language.

cards.title: Not every change is an amendment
cards.body: Making a new State, changing a boundary or changing a **name** is done under **Article 3** by an ordinary law. Kerala became **Keralam** this way in 2026, and Orissa became Odisha in 2011. Article 368 is not used.

cards.q: What does the Constitution call the budget, and under which Article?
What is a Vote on Account?
cards.a: An advance grant to run the government until the budget is passed
cards.n: Asked in 2018. It usually covers two months.

cards.q: Which Bill allows the government to take money out of the Consolidated Fund of India?

cards.title: Three purses
cards.body: The Union keeps its money in three places. The **Consolidated Fund** holds all taxes and loans; nothing leaves it without a law of Parliament. The **Public Account** holds money that belongs to others, such as provident funds. The **Contingency Fund** is a small purse for emergencies, in the hands of the President.

cards.q: Which Article defines a Money Bill?
In which House must a Money Bill be introduced?
cards.n: And only on the recommendation of the President.

cards.q: Who decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
cards.a: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
cards.n: The Speaker’s decision is final.

cards.q: For how many days can the Rajya Sabha keep a Money Bill?
What can the Lok Sabha do with changes the Rajya Sabha suggests to a Money Bill?
cards.n: Asked in 2025. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend.

cards.q: Can there be a joint sitting of the two Houses on a Money Bill?

cards.title: Why the Rajya Sabha is weak on money
cards.body: The Lok Sabha is elected directly by the people who pay the taxes. So on a **Money Bill** the Rajya Sabha can neither reject nor change it. It can only suggest, and it must send the Bill back within **14 days**. If it sits on the Bill, the Bill is taken as passed.

cards.q: Under which Article is a joint sitting of the two Houses held, and who presides?
cards.a: Article 108; the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
cards.n: A joint sitting has been held only three times.

cards.q: A policy cut motion reduces a demand to how much?
cards.n: It says: we reject the whole policy behind this demand.

cards.q: A token cut motion reduces a demand by how much?
cards.n: It is used to air one particular complaint.

cards.title: Three cut motions
cards.body: **Policy cut**: reduce the demand **to ₹1**; we reject the policy. **Economy cut**: reduce it **by a stated sum**; you are spending too much. **Token cut**: reduce it **by ₹100**; we have one complaint. Watch the small words “to” and “by“.

cards.q: Under which Article is the Comptroller and Auditor General appointed, and by whom?
What is the term of office of the CAG?
cards.a: Six years or till the age of 65

cards.q: To whom does the CAG submit his reports on the Union’s accounts?
cards.n: The President places them before Parliament. For a State, the reports go to the Governor.

cards.q: How can the CAG be removed from office?
cards.a: In the same way as a judge of the Supreme Court

cards.q: Who is the present Comptroller and Auditor General of India?

cards.title: The guardian of the public purse
cards.body: The **CAG** checks every rupee the Centre and the States spend. To keep him free, the Constitution gives him a fixed term (**six years or 65**), makes him as hard to remove as a Supreme Court judge, and bars him from any government job afterwards. Ambedkar called him the most important officer under the Constitution.

cards.q: How many members does the Public Accounts Committee have, and from which Houses?
cards.a: 22: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha

cards.q: Who is called the “friend, philosopher and guide” of the Public Accounts Committee?
By convention, the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee comes from which side?
cards.n: The Speaker appoints him. A minister cannot be a member.

cards.q: How many members does the Estimates Committee have, and from which House?

cards.title: Two committees on money
cards.body: The **Public Accounts Committee** (22 members, both Houses) looks back: was the money spent as Parliament ordered? It works from the CAG’s reports. The **Estimates Committee** (30 members, Lok Sabha only) looks forward: could the same work be done for less?

cards.q: Under which Article is the Finance Commission set up, and how often?
cards.n: It advises how taxes should be shared between the Centre and the States.

cards.q: Who chairs the Sixteenth Finance Commission?
Who appoints the Governor of a State, and under which Article?
For how long does a Governor hold office?
cards.a: During the pleasure of the President
cards.n: The normal term is five years, but the President can remove or transfer a Governor at any time.

cards.q: Can a Governor be impeached?
cards.n: Only the President can be impeached. The State Assembly has no power to remove a Governor.

cards.q: What is the minimum age to be a Governor?
Which amendment allowed one person to be Governor of two or more States?
Who gives the oath of office to a Governor?
cards.a: The Chief Justice of the High Court

cards.title: Elected by nobody
cards.body: The Governor is the head of the State, yet no one in the State votes for him. The **President appoints** him (Article 155) and he stays at the **President’s pleasure** (Article 156). The makers copied this from Canada, because they feared an elected Governor would clash with the elected Chief Minister.

cards.q: Which commission said that a Governor should be a non-partisan person from outside the State?
cards.n: Asked in 2025. It was set up in 1983 to study Centre–State relations.

cards.q: Which later commission, set up in 2007, also studied Centre–State relations?
Who was named Governor of Odisha in October 2026?
cards.n: He followed Hari Babu Kambhampati.

cards.q: In which city is the High Court of Odisha, and in which year was it set up?
How many seats does Odisha have in the State Assembly, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha?

cards.title: A minister Odisha must have
cards.body: Article 164 says that in four States there must be a **Minister in charge of tribal welfare**: **Odisha**, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. The same Article says the Governor appoints the Chief Minister, and the other ministers on the Chief Minister’s advice.

cards.q: Article 164 says four States must have a Minister for tribal welfare. Name them.
cards.a: Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand

cards.q: How many States have a Legislative Council today?
Name the six States that have a Legislative Council.
cards.a: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra and Karnataka

cards.q: Does Odisha have a Legislative Council?
cards.n: The Odisha Assembly asked for one in 2018, but Parliament has not made the law.

cards.q: Under which Article is a Legislative Council created or abolished, and by whom?
cards.n: First the State Assembly must pass a resolution by a special majority. Asked in 2021.

cards.q: What are the largest and smallest sizes allowed for a Legislative Council?
cards.a: One-third of the Assembly; at least 40 members

cards.title: Who sits in a Council
cards.body: A Legislative Council is filled in five ways. **One-third** are chosen by the MLAs. **One-third** by local bodies. **One-twelfth** by graduates. **One-twelfth** by teachers. The last **one-sixth** are named by the Governor. A member sits for six years.

cards.title: The House that Odisha asked for
cards.body: Odisha has one House, the Assembly of 147 members. In **2018** that Assembly passed a resolution asking for a second House, a Legislative Council. Under **Article 169** that is only the first step. The second step belongs to **Parliament**, which must pass a law to create the Council. Parliament has not done so. So the resolution lies in Delhi, and Odisha remains one of the twenty-two States with a single House.

cards.q: What is the minimum age to be a member of the Lok Sabha or a State Assembly?
What is the minimum age to be a member of the Rajya Sabha or a Legislative Council?
cards.n: Asked in 2025.

cards.q: What is the minimum age to be a member of a Panchayat or a Municipality?
What is the minimum age to be President or Vice-President of India?

cards.title: The ladder of ages
cards.body: **18** to vote. **21** for a Panchayat or Municipality. **25** for the Lok Sabha or an Assembly. **30** for the Rajya Sabha or a Council. **35** for President, Vice-President or Governor.

cards.q: Under which Article does a Governor issue ordinances, and under which does the President?
Under which Article does the Governor have the power to pardon, and under which does the President?
Who is the highest law officer of a State, and under which Article?
cards.n: The Centre’s law officer is the Attorney General, under Article 76.

cards.q: Which Articles deal with the Public Service Commissions?
Who appoints the chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission?
Who can remove the chairman or a member of a State Public Service Commission?
cards.n: The Governor appoints but cannot remove. For misbehaviour, the Supreme Court must first hold an inquiry.

cards.q: What is the term of a member of the UPSC?
cards.a: Six years or till the age of 65

cards.q: What is the term of a member of a State Public Service Commission?
cards.a: Six years or till the age of 62

cards.q: Who creates a Joint Public Service Commission for two or more States?
cards.n: Asked in 2025. It acts when the State Legislatures ask for it.

cards.q: After retiring, can the chairman of the UPSC take another job under the government?
cards.n: Asked in 2021. A State chairman can still become chairman or member of the UPSC.

cards.title: Appointed here, removed there
cards.body: The **Governor** appoints the members of a State Commission, but only the **President** can remove them. This split is on purpose. A State government that dislikes the Commission’s choice of officers cannot punish it.

cards.title: UPSC and State PSC side by side
cards.body: **Appointed by**: President, Governor. **Removed by**: President in both. **Term**: six years in both. **Age limit**: 65 for the UPSC, **62** for a State Commission. **Report goes to**: President, Governor.

cards.title: Odisha Public Service Commission
cards.body: The body that holds the ASO examination was set up on **1 April 1949**. Its office is at **Cuttack**. It works under Articles 315 to 323, like every State Commission.

cards.q: In which year was the Odisha Public Service Commission set up, and where is its office?
In which year was the first Public Service Commission set up in India?
cards.n: The Lee Commission had recommended it in 1924.

cards.title: National Human Rights Commission
cards.body: It was set up under the **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**. So it is a **statutory** body, made by a law, and not a constitutional one.

cards.q: Under which Act was the National Human Rights Commission set up?
Who was the first chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission?
cards.n: Asked in 2021. He was born in Odisha and had been Chief Justice of India.

cards.q: Since 2019, who can be the chairperson of the NHRC?
cards.a: A former Chief Justice of India or a former Supreme Court judge
cards.n: Before 2019 only a former Chief Justice of India could hold the post.

cards.q: What is the term of the NHRC chairperson since 2019?
cards.a: Three years or till the age of 70
cards.n: It was five years before the change.

cards.q: Who is the present chairperson of the NHRC?

cards.title: The Odia judge in the first chair
cards.body: When the National Human Rights Commission opened in **1993**, its first chairperson was **Justice Ranganath Misra**. He was born at Banpur in Odisha and began as a lawyer in Cuttack. He rose to be a judge of the Orissa High Court, then of the Supreme Court, and in 1990 the **Chief Justice of India**. In those days only a former Chief Justice could head the Commission. That rule was relaxed in **2019**.

cards.q: How many members sit on the committee that recommends the NHRC chairperson, and who heads it?
Name the six members of the committee that selects the NHRC chairperson.
cards.a: PM, Speaker, Home Minister, both Leaders of the Opposition, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha
cards.n: The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha is not on it. That was the trap in 2025.

cards.q: Who appoints the chairperson of the NHRC?
Which Article sets up the Election Commission of India?
What is the term of the Chief Election Commissioner?
cards.a: Six years or till the age of 65

cards.q: How can the Chief Election Commissioner be removed?
cards.a: In the same way as a judge of the Supreme Court

cards.q: Who was the first Chief Election Commissioner of India?
On which date is National Voters’ Day kept, and why?
cards.a: 25 January; the Election Commission was founded on that day in 1950

cards.title: In the book or made by a law?
cards.body: **Constitutional** bodies have their own Article: the Election Commission (324), UPSC (315), Finance Commission (280), CAG (148). **Statutory** bodies were made by an Act: the NHRC, the Central Information Commission, the Lokpal. **NITI Aayog** is neither. It was made by a Cabinet resolution.

cards.q: Is the National Human Rights Commission a constitutional body or a statutory body?
NITI Aayog was created by which means?
cards.a: A resolution of the Union Cabinet
cards.n: So it is neither constitutional nor statutory. It replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
